first.rationale: Triage logic: the two beliefs that are both most consequential to this week's single slot and least supported for the stated objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue) are memory_73 and memory_86. memory_73 is the direct competitive counter to the entry-pricing attack and would be the highest-pull option, but its record only claims acquisition and revenue lift; it is silent on retention, discount-cohort margin, and whether the revenue was qualified or churn-prone — exactly the failure mode that converts a short-term win into long-term value erosion. memory_86 is the belief I currently intend to act on, and its endpoints (completion rate, time-to-value, 'early product adoption') are activation proxies, not downstream qualified revenue; simplifying signup can raise completion while lowering lead quality, so I need the original record to see whether any revenue-side metric was tracked and over what horizon. memory_31 is nearly redundant with memory_86 (same mechanism, weaker scope), memory_57 and memory_44 address segments that are not the source of this quarter's decline, and memory_91 is cheap and reversible enough that verifying it would not change the decision. Intended action is simplify_onboarding because onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%) are both down and the funnel step is upstream of both, whereas promotional pricing responds to the competitor on their chosen terrain and risks repricing the base. I am running it as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout precisely because the supporting evidence is proxy-based: the test should carry downstream qualified-revenue and retention instrumentation, not just completion rate, and a pre-committed stop if lead quality degrades. If archive retrieval shows memory_86 was validated only on completion with no revenue follow-through, or shows memory_73 tracked retention cleanly and held up, I will revise before committing.

final.rationale: The archive resolved the decision in the direction I had provisionally weighted, and it did so by falsifying the one option that would otherwise have been most tempting. exp_73 shows targeted discounting bought +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue at the cost of -12% 30-day retention, with the original analyst explicitly warning against generalizing it as a sustainable-growth strategy. The inherited memory_73 summary had lossily dropped that retention figure and that warning, retaining only the favorable half. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is now ruled out on its own evidence, not on my prior: it purchases a cohort that does not survive the first renewal cycle, which is value destruction dressed as acquisition. Meeting the competitor's entry pricing would also reprice the existing base and invite a margin race I have no evidence of winning. exp_86 came back confirmed and, importantly, stronger than the summary: it carries a retention endpoint (+3% at 30 days) alongside completion (+13%) and time-to-value (-2.1 days). That materially reduces my main worry, which was that shortened onboarding lifts a funnel proxy while quietly degrading lead quality. A positive retention signal is the opposite of that failure mode. Onboarding completion is down 4% and activation down 6%; onboarding sits upstream of both, so the intervention targets the actual mechanism of this quarter's decline rather than the competitor's chosen terrain. I am raising scale from small_guarded_test to standard_experiment because the verified record now supports the mechanism on a retention endpoint, but not to broad_rollout: exp_86's horizon is 30 days, and the objective is long-term qualified revenue, so the evidence still stops short of the endpoint I actually care about. Residual uncertainty I am carrying forward rather than resolving: whether the retention lift persists past first renewal, and whether a shortened flow behaves the same under competitive pressure that is currently changing the composition of inbound SMB traffic. Instrumentation must therefore include downstream qualified revenue and renewal-cycle retention by cohort, not completion rate alone, with a pre-committed stop if lead quality degrades. I am also flagging for the durable record that memory_73 should be rewritten to carry the retention loss and the analyst's do-not-generalize conclusion, since the lossy version came within one verification pull of driving the wrong call, and memory_57's 'no measurable harm to retention' claim now deserves the same scrutiny before anyone acts on it.
